newsitem.title: JAPAN: Publisher defies ban on Japan murder suspect photo.
newsitem.headline: Publisher defies ban on Japan murder suspect photo.

text.p: Japan's Justice Ministry demanded on Friday that a publishing firm withdraw two news weeklies carrying photos of a 14-year-old boy accused of the brutal murder of a boy three years younger.
But Shinchosha, publisher of the weekly magazines Focus and Shukan Shincho refused, saying the demand violated the freedom of the press.
The row is the latest twist in a murder case that has shocked Japan.
Police arrested the 14-year-old last Saturday on suspicion of murdering 11-year-old Jun Hase in Kobe, western Japan.

Jun's severed head was found at the gate of a junior high school on May 27 with a note stuck in the mouth saying the killer was taking revenge against the education system. Jun had been strangled to death before being decapitated.
Japan's Juvenile Law bans publishers from revealing the name or printing photographs of a minor -- in Japan anyone aged 19 or younger -- suspected of involvement in a criminal case.
But the law does not provide a penalty for offenders.
"The publications clearly violate the Juvenile Law," Justice Minister Isao Matsuura told a news conference. "This also severely violates the privacy and rights of the suspected minor.

"Despite our serious warnings in a similar, earlier case against the same publisher, it repeated the offence. The publisher does not have respect for human rights and its attitude of ignoring the law is excessive," Matsuura said.
Formally called an "official recommendation", the justice minister's demand cannot be enforced, ministry officials said.

When the latest issue of the news weekly Focus hit news stands on Tuesday carrying a photograph of the suspect, the magazine came under a hail of protests from lawyers, civic groups and government leaders.
Despite the outcry, Shinchosha raised the stakes by printing the same photograph in Shukan Shincho, or the Weekly Shincho, a day later, this time with a black slit across the eyes.
Shinchosha said editors decided to carry the photograph of the suspect because it was an exceptional case.
Teruo Kosuge, deputy editor of Shukan Shincho, said the latest move by the justice minister violated the freedom of the press.
"We published the article after taking full account of the fact that the boy was under protection under the Juvenile Law," he said in a statement.
"This unilateral decision to withdraw the magazines interferes with freedom of press and expression and we will not accept this recommendation," Kosuge said.
Soon after the arrest, the chief of Kobe police's homicide squad said the suspect had told investigators he strangled Jun and cut off his head with a saw.
Police also said the suspect told investigators he assaulted two small girls in the neighbourhood in March, one of whom died of stab wounds.
In 1985, Focus published a photograph of a 16-year-old boy suspected of killing both his parents.
At that time the Justice Ministry issued a similar "official recommendation" calling on the publisher to respect children's rights, but did not demand that it withdraw the magazine.
